alt: Three stacked cards: Part One, Self-discovery; Part Two, Between us; Part Three, Understanding people, with arrows showing how they connect.
caption: How the three parts fit together: you bring yourself into every shared life, and Part Three explains why the Part Two tools work.

alt: A simple building whose roof rests on five columns, one for each of the five ideas the book rests on.
caption: Five ideas the whole book rests on. Each one starts inside you, then shows up between you and the people you share a life with.

alt: A timeline with three stops, Then, Now and Next, and the line: the past isn’t yours to change; what you carry forward is.
caption: Where your lens came from, how you run today and who you are becoming, in one picture. You choose what you carry forward.

alt: Three stacked layers: today’s conditions (work around it), patterns life taught you (work on it, kindly) and your wiring (work with it).
caption: Three layers in every reaction. Each one changes at a different speed and needs a different move.

alt: A winding path with eight stops from birth to later life, each with the question that stage of life asks.
caption: Each stage of life asks its own question. The ages are rough, and the questions come back at big changes (after Erik Erikson).

alt: Four numbered steps: name it, now or older, which layer, what does it need.
caption: A four-step self-check for a feeling that is bigger than you expected. Do it once the first wave has passed.

alt: Three rings: in your hands at the center, what you can influence around it, and what is not yours to decide on the outside.
caption: Your circle of control. Spend your energy from the middle out. Most exhaustion comes from pouring it into the outer ring.

alt: Seven stepping stones from “what matters to me?” to “look back kindly,” with an arrow going around again.
caption: A kind plan for change in seven small steps. If the plan isn’t working, change the plan, not your opinion of yourself.

alt: An iceberg: the doing shows above the water; noticing, remembering, planning and deciding, checking and smoothing sit unseen below.
caption: The work nobody sees. Most of a job happens before and after the doing, and whoever holds that part can never fully switch off.

alt: Two bars: one person thinks they do about 60 percent, the other about 55 percent; together they add up to 115 percent of the same work.
caption: We each remember our own effort best. Illustrative numbers. In Ross and Sicoly’s 1979 study, partners’ estimates of their own share usually added up to more than 100 percent.

alt: Two wave lines at nearly the same speed add up to a third pattern that swells and fades, a whistle neither one sent.
caption: The radio whistle. Two reasonable signals, nearly in step, can make a clash that neither person started: it started between you.

alt: Four numbered steps: name the mismatch without blame, check your own state, slow the pace, then go back to the topic.
caption: Retuning, step by step, before you carry on with a talk that has started to whistle.

alt: Three bars show what each input could earn and did earn in a made-up week; they add up to 0.67, marked on a scale from 0 to 1 in the middle, “drifting” band.
caption: Is the split working? Three readings go in and one snapshot comes out. Start with the biggest shortfall. It judges the setup, never a person.

alt: A tank filled in layers by five scores (sleep debt, workload elsewhere, unresolved conflict, body, time pressure), reaching 0.55, in the medium band.
caption: How full is your stress tank? Five things scored 0 to 4, added up and divided by 20. The scores shown are an example. The items and bands are this book’s.

alt: A circle labeled “the same moment” with seven circles around it: tiredness, time pressure, history, family script, fairness, talking style and outside stress.
caption: Seven angles on the same moment. An angle is a place to stand, not a verdict: name your own, and ask about theirs.

alt: Two cards, fair by results and fair by promises, each with a small job list, and a tag showing a job with a named owner and a second name.
caption: Two kinds of fair. Both are reasonable. Trouble starts when people use different ones without saying so. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner.

alt: Three steps, notice, name it out loud, decide once settled; then two boxes separating a fact question from a reaction question.
caption: Let a comment land before you react: notice, name, decide. And keep the fact question apart from the feeling question.

alt: A grid of jobs by week with crosses where a job slipped, then three kinds of gap with what to do about each, then counting and closing the month.
caption: The monthly look-back: mark the month, sort each repeat, count and close. The ✗ goes next to a job, never a person.

alt: A simple figure with five places feelings often show up first, and three steps: feel it, name it, choose.
caption: A feeling is a signal, not a verdict. It often shows up in the body first. Naming it helps you choose what to do next.

alt: Three bands, revved up, calm and connected, and running on empty, with a line showing one afternoon moving through them.
caption: The ladder: three everyday states. You move up and down it all day. Hard talks go best from the middle band.

alt: A curve of body alarm that crosses a “flooded” line, then comes down during a break of twenty minutes or more; a dashed line shows pushing on keeps it high.
caption: Flooded means offline. Pause and name a time to come back, settle the body for at least twenty minutes, then talk. Illustrative curve.

alt: What happened passes through three filters, expectation, attention and mood, and comes out as a story; a side path says ask, don’t guess.
caption: Seeing is a best guess. The story that comes out feels like a fact. Asking is kinder and more accurate than reading minds.

alt: Three speech bubbles: what was said, what was meant, and what was heard, ending with a check question.
caption: Every message says two things: the words, and what they seem to say about the two of you. Check, don’t guess.

alt: Three blocks, what happened, how I feel, what I’d like, each with an example sentence, and a crossed-out criticism.
caption: Say it so it lands: what happened, how I feel, what I’d like. A complaint about an action can be heard. A criticism of the person starts a defense.

alt: A square field with avoidance across and anxiety up, dots spread across it, and an arrow showing that a person’s place can shift.
caption: Attachment as two scales, not four boxes: worry about being left, and unease with closeness. Everyone sits somewhere, and can move. Dots are illustrative.

alt: Two boxes in a loop: one person reaches harder, the other pulls back, each move making the other’s stronger.
caption: When one reaches and one pulls back. Nobody is the villain. The way out is to soften the reaching and to say when you’ll come back.

alt: A loop of three circles: cue, routine, reward.
caption: Habits run on cues. Over time the cue alone is enough, so change the setup, not just your willpower.

alt: Three rising curves that level off, reaching 95 percent of their own plateau at about 18, 66 and 254 days; a small dip shows a missed day is not a reset.
caption: How long a new habit takes to feel automatic: about two months on average, with a very wide range. Illustrative shapes based on Lally and colleagues (2010).

alt: One mistake splits into two roads: guilt leads to owning it, saying sorry and putting it right; shame leads to hiding, blaming or lashing out. Self-compassion is the bridge.
caption: Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.” Guilt is easier to put right, and self-compassion helps you cross over.

alt: A line swinging between a loss lane and a restoration lane over time, with a sudden spike set off by a song or a date.
caption: Grief comes in waves, not neat stages. Moving back and forth between loss and everyday life is part of healthy grieving.

alt: A crossed-out line from “less” to “more,” and a six-spoke wheel with two different, uneven profile shapes.
caption: Brains vary, like bodies do. A mind has a profile with its own shape, not a place on a line from “a little” to “a lot.” Different, not broken.

alt: A winding path toward a value that points off the page, with goals as flags and small everyday acts as dots, and a compass beside it.
caption: Values are directions, not finish lines. Goals are stops on the way. Missing one doesn’t change the direction.

alt: A loop of four boxes: in step, a break, repair, back in step; below, three parts of a real apology.
caption: Every close relationship has breaks. What counts is the repair. A real apology names it, owns it and mends it.

alt: A speech bubble asking “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” above four tiles: listening, practical, ideas, making sense.
caption: Ask what kind of help they want. Fixing it for them can take away their power, and your limits make your help last.

alt: A thermometer with four levels, irritated, annoyed, angry and the hot minutes, each with what helps at that level.
caption: Anger rises fast, and what helps depends on how hot it is. In the hot minutes, slow the body first. Letting rip feeds it.

alt: Five rows, one per Big Five trait, each a line between two plain-language ends with a hump showing most people near the middle.
caption: Traits work like sliders, and most people sit near the middle of each. Illustrative shapes.

alt: Five hearts for friends, family, partners, chosen family and yourself, above a loop: you share, they respond, you feel known.
caption: Closeness grows from being known: you share something real, the other person responds with understanding, and you share a little more.

alt: A loop of fear, avoiding and quick relief, then a staircase of small planned steps leading to “I went, and I coped.”
caption: Avoiding keeps fear going. Small, planned steps back in help most.

alt: A line-matching card and two rows of people: alone against a group giving the wrong answer, and with one ally giving the right one.
caption: We go along more than we think, and one other voice changes a lot. In Asch’s studies, going along fell sharply when one other person gave the right answer.

alt: Three panels for the three parts with six colored threads running across all of them, each labeled with one of the book’s six threads.
caption: Six threads that run through the whole book, from the first chapters to the last.
